sets.title: Mock F · Paper 1
sets.desc: Real CFA Institute Level II Mock 4, Session 1: vignettes, questions and explanations as published (44 questions, 2 h 12 min).

vignettes.body:
George Hansen manages portfolios for high-net-worth clients based in the US. He meets with a client who recently inherited a portfolio with investments in both a REIT and a commodity futures fund.
REIT
Hansen reviews the client's investment in Maipo Valley Group, a retail REIT located in the US. Hansen uses the information in Exhibit 1 to calculate Maipo's net asset value per share (NAVPS).
Exhibit 1
Last-12-month pro forma cash net operating income (NOI) | $240 million
Next-12-month growth in NOI | $36 million
Cash and equivalents | $10 million
Accounts receivable | $25 million
Prepaid/Other assets | $15 million
Land held for future development | $800 million
Total debt | $600 million
Market capitalization | $2,250 million
Shares outstanding | 50 million
Capitalization rate | 8.0%
Cost of equity | 9.5%
Dividend payout ratio | 100.0%
Managed Commodity Futures Fund
Hansen then reviews the investment in the Crescent commodity futures fund. The fund currently holds positions in the natural gas, softs (cash crops), and livestock sectors.
Hansen observes that Crescent's returns in the natural gas sector behaved differently from the other two sectors over the past five years. According to Crescent's prospectus, the fund always takes a long position in the natural gas futures contract with the shortest maturity. At the contract maturity date, Crescent rolls forward the existing contract to the new contract with the shortest maturity. Hansen gathers in Exhibit 2 prior-year price information for the natural gas market for two of Crescent's trade dates. All prices are in $ per million British thermal units as of the date listed.
Exhibit 2
# Trade Date | Spot Price | June Futures Price | July Futures Price | August Futures Price
28 May | 1.795 | 1.957 | 2.418 | 2.793
26 June | 1.795 | 1.795 | 2.338 | 2.546

questions.q: Maipo's NAVPS is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because NOI is valued at the cost of equity, not the cap rate:
Last-12-month pro forma cash net operating income (NOI)	$240
Plus: Next-12-month growth in NOI 	$36
Equals: Estimated next-12-month cash NOI	$276
Incorrectly divide the above number by cost of equity of 9.5% to get:
Estimated value of operating real estate ($276/0.095)	$2,905.26
Plus: Cash, Accounts Receivable, and Prepaid Assets	$50
Plus: Land held for future development 	$800
Equals: Estimated gross asset value	$3,755.26
Less: Total debt 	$600
Equals: Net asset value (NAV)	$3,155.26
Divide by: Number of shares 	50
Equals: NAVPS	$63.11
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because debt is not subtracted from the estimated value of operating real estate when NAVPS is calculated:
Last-12-month pro forma cash net operating income (NOI)	$240
Plus: Next-12-month growth in NOI	$36
Equals: Estimated next-12-month cash NOI	$276
Divide above number by the cap rate of 8.0% to get:
Estimated value of operating real estate ($276/0.08)	$3,450
Plus: Cash, Accounts Receivable, and Prepaid Assets	$50
Plus: Land held for future development	$800
Equals: Estimated gross asset value	$4,300
Less: Total debt (Omitted)	 
Equals: Net asset value	$4,300
Divide by: Number of shares	50
Equals: NAVPS	$86
This also rounds up from $85.50 which you get if you add the cash, accounts receivable, and prepaid assets before applying the cap rate (and subtract total debt correctly).

questions.q: Which of the following factors is most likely a primary influence for all three commodity sectors held by Crescent?
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because spoilage has very little effect on the supply of natural gas. Spoilage does affect the supply for the softs and livestock sectors. 
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because consumer preferences are not a primary influence on natural gas.
Demand for natural gas is driven primarily by weather conditions (heating and cooling) and only secondarily by industrial activity.

questions.q: The roll return on Crescent's natural gas futures contract on the 26 June trade date was:
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because the roll return would equal zero only if the June and July futures prices were equal on 26 June, which is not the case since the June price is $1.795 and the July price is $2.338.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because the roll return is negative when the numerator is correctly calculated as (Near-term futures contract closing price − Farther-term futures contract closing price). The roll return is only positive if the numerator calculation is incorrectly reversed: (Farther-term futures contract closing price − Near-term futures contract closing price) = $2.338 – $1.795 = $0.543 > 0.

questions.q: Under the hedging pressure hypothesis, the prices in Exhibit 2 indicate:
options: excess demand for price protection by producers.
excess demand for price protection by consumers.
balanced demand for price protection by producers and consumers.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because if commodity producers as a group are more interested in selling forward (seeking price insurance) than commodity consumers (as per the concept of normal backwardation) are, then the shape and structure of the futures price curve can be illustrated as backwardation.
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because if the two forces of producers and consumers both seeking price protection are equal in weight, then a flat futures curve is produced. However, in this case the futures curve is upward sloping and so the demand must not be balanced.

vignettes.body:
Fei Yang is a portfolio manager analyzing fixed-income investments in various currencies.
Yang begins by analyzing investment opportunities in Country 1. She has a 2-year investment horizon and evaluates the following two strategies, each of which uses government bonds with a 4.00% annual coupon and a par value of $100.
Strategy A: Purchase a 2-year bond and hold it to maturity
Strategy B: Purchase a 3-year bond and sell it in two years
Yang uses the spot rates for Country 1 government bonds, shown in Exhibit 1, to evaluate these strategies. Yang expects the shape and level of the yield curve in Country 1 to remain unchanged over her investment horizon.
Exhibit 1
# Term (Years) | Spot Rate
1 | 3.00%
2 | 5.00%
3 | 7.00%
For Country 2, Yang anticipates that economic growth will accelerate. As a result, she expects Country 2's yield curve, which is currently upward sloping, to rise and become steeper than currently expected by the market. Given her expectations, Yang considers which of the three compositions for her long–only government bond portfolio in Exhibit 2 would be the most appropriate.
Exhibit 2
# Portfolio | Short-Term Bonds | Intermediate-Term Bonds | Long-Term Bonds
1 | 80% | 10% | 10%
2 | 33% | 34% | 33%
3 | 45% | 10% | 45%
Yang then considers Country 3 and calculates the 5-year swap spread, based on a 5-year swap rate of 5.50% and the data on recently issued government bonds shown in Exhibit 3.
Exhibit 3
# Government Bond | Original Maturity | Remaining Maturity | Yield-to-Maturity
Bond A | 5.0 years | 4.0 years | 5.20%
Bond B | 5.0 years | 4.5 years | 5.30%
Bond C | 6.0 years | 5.5 years | 5.40%

questions.q: The YTM for the bond in Strategy A is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because this calculation is based on getting the correct price of the bond (98.21) but then assuming that the YTM involves multiplying the amortized discount by a factor of two (for a two-year bond).
[(100/98.21) – 1] × 2 = 3.65%
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because this is the average of the 1- and 2-year spot rates (3.00%, 5.00%). It is also the coupon rate (4.00%). Neither of these approaches correctly uses the spot rates to value the bond's cash flows.
C. Correct.

questions.q: Given Yang's expectation for the yield curve in Country 1, the expected total return for Strategy A over her investment horizon is:
options: less than that of Strategy B.
equal to that of Strategy B.
greater than that of Strategy B.
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because the total return for a buy-and-hold strategy (Strategy A) will be less than that of 'rolling down the yield curve' (Strategy B) when the yield curve is upward sloping and expected to remain unchanged over the investment horizon.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because the total return from 'rolling down the yield curve' (Strategy B) is higher than that of buy-and-hold (Strategy A).

questions.q: Given Yang expectations for Country 2's yield curve, the most appropriate bond portfolio composition would be:
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because Portfolio 2, whose composition is evenly spread across a range of maturities, is a 'laddered portfolio', will have a higher portfolio duration than Portfolio 1. Given rising yields and a steeper yield curve, Yang will want to have a portfolio with the shortest duration possible.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because Portfolio 3 is a barbell portfolio with a greater weighting to long-term bonds than Portfolio 1 (45% compared with 10%). As a result, its portfolio duration will be longer than that of Portfolio 1. Given the expectation of a rising and steepening yield curve, Yang will want to have a portfolio with the shortest duration possible.

questions.q: The 5-year swap spread in Country 3 is:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because this is the spread between the swap rate the interpolated YTMs of the bonds with the 4.5-year and 5.5-year remaining maturities, Bonds B and C.
0.15% = 5.50% – (5.30% + 5.40%) / 2
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because this is calculated from the interpolated YTMs of the bonds with the 4.0-year and 4.5-year remaining maturities, but which were both originally issued as 5-year bonds, Bonds A and B:
0.25% = 5.50% – (5.20% + 5.30%) / 2

vignettes.body:
Debra McAlister is an equity analyst for a mutual fund company. She is researching two equities, Zedco Inc. and Midord Corporation, as possible additions to the firm's portfolios.
Zedco Inc.
Zedco's average ROE is the highest in its industry, but it has been volatile. McAlister is concerned about using past data to estimate the company's future ROE. Zedco has an average level of debt for its industry but, in response to lower interest rates, is expected to refinance most of its older debt within the next year. In developing her valuation, McAlister is uncertain about her estimate of Zedco's terminal value. Zedco has a low dividend payout ratio, which McAlister expects to be maintained. Finally, compared to its historical financial statements, Zedco's most recent financial statement shows an abnormally high level of accounting accruals.
McAlister decides to use both single-stage and multistage residual income models to value Zedco. To check her assumptions, McAlister calculates the implied growth rate in Zedco's residual income using its current market price. She uses the data in Exhibit 1 for her analysis.
Exhibit 1
Cost of equity capital | 12%
WACC | 10%
ROE (3-year average) | 29%
Current price per share | $80
Book value per share | $20
Midord Corporation
Based on Midord's characteristics, McAlister decides to estimate its value using both a two-stage DDM and the H-model. For both models, she uses a required return on equity of 10% and Midord's most recent dividend payment of $0.55 per share. For the two-stage DDM, McAlister uses Midord's trailing P/E ratio to estimate its terminal value per share in Year 8 with the following additional assumptions:
Annual growth in dividends in years 1 through 8 = 12%
Dividend payout ratio at the end of Year 8 = 60%
Trailing P/E ratio at the end of Year 8 = 20
For the H-model, McAlister's additional model inputs are:
Half-life of the high-growth period (H) = 4 years
Initial short-term dividend growth rate (gS) = 12%
Long-term dividend growth rate (gL) = 5%

questions.q: Which of the following best supports McAlister's choice of valuation models for Zedco?
options: The estimation of Zedco's terminal value
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because Zedco has the highest average ROE in its industry, but it has been volatile, and McAlister is not highly confident in using past data to estimate future ROE. ROE is a critical input to the residual income model, so an uncertain estimate of ROE would not support the use of the residual income model. Residual income models are least appropriate when significant determinants of residual income, such as book value and ROE, are not predictable.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because Zedco is expected to refinance most of its older debt within the year in response to lower interest rates. This implies that the interest cost on the most recent income statement does not accurately reflect the current cost of debt. One of the potential weaknesses of the residual income model is that: The residual income model’s use of accounting income assumes that the cost of debt capital is reflected appropriately by interest expense.
C. Correct.

questions.q: Using the single-stage residual income model, Zedco's implied growth rate in residual income is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because the WACC (10%) is used in place of the cost of equity capital:
0.10 – [(0.29 – 0.10)/($80/$20 – 1)] = 0.03667 ≈ 3.7%.
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because the "–1" is omitted from the denominator:
0.12 – [(0.29 – 0.12)/($80/$20)] = 0.0775 ≈ 7.8%.

questions.q: Using the two-stage DDM, the estimated terminal value per share for Midord is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because the dividend payout ratio is multiplied instead of divided.
TV = 20 × $0.55 × [(1.12)8 × 0.60] = $16.34 ≈ $16.
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because (1 – D/E) or the retention ratio is used instead of the dividend payout ratio.
TV = 20 × $0.55 × [(1.12)8/(1 – 0.60)] = $68.09 ≈ $68.

vignettes.body:
Susan Park, CFA, is a portfolio manager at Plum Asset Management. Plum has adopted the Standards as part of its ethics and compliance policy, but does not claim compliance with the GIPS standards.
When preparing reports relating to performance presentation for her clients, Park applies the following criteria:
Criterion 1: Performance is presented using a weighted composite of similar portfolios.
Criterion 2: Terminated accounts are excluded from the calculation of performance history.
Criterion 3: Performance presentations are tailored to the knowledge and sophistication of the client.
Park receives orders from four of her clients to purchase shares in an oversubscribed IPO. She determines that the IPO is suitable for all of these clients. One of the clients, a family member of Park's, has a regular fee-paying account that is managed similarly to those of the other three clients. Park allocates the shares she receives to the four clients on a pro rata basis according to order size. She discloses the firm's IPO allocation policy to only those clients that participate in IPOs.
Park meets with a prospective client. During their initial meeting, Park makes the following statements to the client:
Statement 1: "I passed all three levels of the CFA exam on my first attempt."
Statement 2: "The CFA Program has enhanced my portfolio management skills."
Statement 3: "As a CFA charterholder, I am the most qualified to manage your investments."
After their initial meeting, Park and the prospective client visit an inexpensive cafe. During their meal, the prospective client states that he is impressed with Plum's services and indicates that he will open an account with Plum. The client offers Park to use the client's vacation home for a week whenever she outperforms the benchmark index in a given quarter. At the end of the meal, the client insists on paying the cafe bill. Later that day, Park speaks with Plum's compliance officer about the client's offer to use the vacation home. The compliance officer does not raise any objections to the vacation home arrangement and gives verbal consent to use the home. Park also discloses to the compliance officer that the client paid the cafe bill. In the next quarter, Park outperforms the benchmark and then uses the vacation home.

questions.q: Which of Park's criteria is not consistent with the Standard relating to performance presentation?
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because, when a firm does not claim compliance with GIPS, members and candidates can meet their obligations under Standard III(D) Performance Presentation by meeting certain criteria which include: presenting the performance of the weighted composite of similar portfolios rather than using a single representative account. Therefore, Criterion 1 is consistent with the Standard relating to performance presentation.
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because, when a firm does not claim compliance with GIPS, members and candidates can meet their obligations under Standard III(D) Performance Presentation by meeting certain criteria which include: considering the knowledge and sophistication of the audience to whom a performance presentation is addressed. Therefore, Criterion 3 is consistent with the Standard relating to performance presentation.

questions.q: With regard to her actions associated with the IPO, did Park violate the Standard relating to fair dealing?
options: Yes, because she allocated IPO shares to her family member
Yes, because she did not appropriately disclose the firm's IPO allocation policy
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because Park violated Standard III(B) Fair Dealing by not disclosing the trade allocation policy to all clients—she did so to only those clients that participate in IPOs.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because Park's allocation of IPO shares to her family member did not violate Standard III(B) Fair Dealing. Because the family member's account is a regular fee-paying account and is managed similarly to other clients' accounts, it was appropriate to allocate IPO shares to the family member.
If the investment professional’s family-member accounts are managed similarly to the accounts of other clients of the firm, however, the family-member accounts should not be excluded from buying such shares.
C. Correct.

questions.q: Which of Park's statements to the prospective client is a violation of the Standards?
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because, according to Standard VII(B), if a candidate passes each level of the exam in consecutive years and wants to state that he or she did so, that is not a violation of Standard VII(B) because it is a statement of fact.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because Park's statement that completion of the CFA Program has enhanced her portfolio management skills is an example of a proper reference to the CFA designation and allowed under Standard VII(B).
C. Correct.

questions.q: After their initial meeting, are Park's actions with regard to the prospective client a violation of the Standards?
options: Yes, because she did not pay the cafe bill
Yes, because she used the client's vacation home
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because Park did not receive appropriate approval for the vacation home arrangement, so she should not have accepted the offer to use the home. She should have gotten written approval from all parties involved, not just verbal approval.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because, according to Standard IV(B), modest gifts and entertainment are acceptable. A meal at an inexpensive cafe most likely falls within this category.
C. Correct.

vignettes.body:
Evangelia Georgiou is an analyst with a family office. She is researching Rummidge, a publicly listed company, and Gimmerton, a private company.
To analyze Rummidge, Georgiou uses the information in Exhibit 1. She believes that the past seven years reflect average profitability over the company's business cycle. Using the method of average ROE for earnings normalization, Georgiou calculates Rummidge's P/E ratio based on normalized EPS.
Exhibit 1
Current share price | $23.40
Current book value per share | $19.50
Average EPS (past 7 years) | $2.45
Average ROE (past 7 years) | 9.5%
Required rate of return on equity | 9.0%
Forecast long-term dividend payout ratio | 75%
For comparison, Georgiou also determines Rummidge's justified P/B ratio based on her forecasts and using the Gordon growth model. For her calculation, she uses the average ROE for the past seven years as the forecast of long-term future ROE.
Next, the family office asks Georgiou to evaluate a proposal to take a minority stake in Gimmerton. To facilitate comparison with the EBITDA disclosed by its publicly listed peers, Georgiou adjusts Gimmerton's reported EBITDA to account for the following:
• Gimmerton's founder and CEO is paid a fixed annual salary of $0.4 million. A market-based compensation package for a CEO of a similar public company would be $1.0 million.
• Gimmerton owns a luxury yacht that is not required for its core operations. In the last fiscal year, expenses associated with the yacht contributed $1.2 million to operating costs and $0.5 million to depreciation expense.
Georgiou values a 100% equity stake in Gimmerton and then calculates the total discount for the minority stake to incorporate both the lack of control and the lack of marketability. She uses a control premium of 25% and a discount for lack of marketability of 10%.

questions.q: Using the method of average ROE for earnings normalization, Rummidge's P/E ratio based on normalized EPS is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because this is the P/E when EPS is normalized by the method of historical average EPS and not the method of average ROE used by Georgiou. 
The historical average EPS over the past 7 years is $2.45, which is deemed in this case to reflect average profitability over the business cycle.
The current share price is $23.40, so P/E = $23.40/$2.45 = 9.55 ≈ 9.6.
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because this is the P/E when EPS is calculated by multiplying the book value per share by the required rate of return on equity and not the historical average ROE, which is the method used by Georgiou. 
The required rate of return on equity is 9.0% and the book value per share is $19.50, so EPS is 0.09 × $19.50 = $1.755.
P/E is then $23.40/$1.755 = 13.33 ≈ 13.3.

questions.q: Based on Georgiou's forecasts, Rummidge's justified P/B ratio is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because this would be the justified P/B ratio if the numerator and denominator in the formula were switched.
Justified P/B = (r – g)/(ROE – g) 
Justified P/B = (0.09 – 0.02375)/(0.095 – 0.02375) = 0.9298 ≈ 0.93
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because this would be the justified P/B ratio if the dividend payout ratio of 75% was used in the formula instead of the earnings retention rate of 25% as follows: 
g = 75% × 9.5% = 7.125%.
Justified P/B = (0.095 – 0.07125)/(0.09 – 0.07125) = 1.2667 ≈ 1.27

questions.q: To facilitate comparison with publicly listed peers, Georgiou should adjust Gimmerton's EBITDA:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because this is the result if the correct adjustments are identified but incorrectly applied when adjusting reported EBITDA as follows:
Incorrectly adding $0.6 million (with respect to the CEO's salary in excess of the market rate) and subtracting $1.2 million (with respect to the yacht's operating expenses, which are not related to core operations) results in an adjustment of:
$0.6 million – $1.2 million = –$0.6 million.
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because this is the EBITDA adjustment if an adjustment for depreciation of the luxury yacht is also taken into account in addition to the other adjustments. 
Subtracting $0.6 million (with respect to the CEO's salary in excess of the market rate) and adding $1.2 million (with respect to the yacht's operating expenses, which are not related to core activities) and also adding $0.5 million (with respect to depreciation) results in an adjustment of:
–$0.6 million + $1.2 million + $0.5 million = $1.1 million.

questions.q: The total discount that Georgiou should apply when valuing the minority stake in Gimmerton is:
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because the discounts for lack of control and lack of marketability are simply added as follows:
With a control premium of 25%, DLOC = 1 – [1/(1.25)] = 0.20 or 20%.
Total discount = DLOC + DLOM = 20% + 10% = 30%
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because the control premium is used instead of the discount for lack of control as follows:
Total discount = 1 – [(1 – Control premium) × (1 – DLOM)] = 1 – [(1 – 0.25) × (1 – 0.10)]
= 0.325 or 32.5%

vignettes.body:
Isabelle Boyer is a fund-of-funds portfolio manager based in Ireland. She is assessing the performance of active asset managers across different regions over the previous quarter, and is planning her fund's tactical allocation for the next quarter.
Boyer begins by looking at Polari, an active US equity manager. She analyzes Polari's performance for the previous quarter using the Carhart four-factor model, which includes the following factors: market return minus risk-free rate (RMRF), small minus big (SMB), high minus low (HML), and winners minus losers (WML).
Exhibit 1 illustrates factor sensitivities and factor returns for Polari and its benchmark over the previous quarter. Polari’s active return for the quarter was 2.5%. Boyer uses this information to assess the investment style of the manager and to decompose the active returns into the return from factor tilts and from security selection.
Exhibit 1
# Factor | Factor Sensitivity for Polari | Factor Sensitivity for Benchmark | Factor Return
RMRF | 1.1 | 1.0 | 5.0%
SMB | 0.3 | 0.0 | –2.0%
HML | 0.4 | 0.2 | 1.0%
WML | –0.1 | 0.1 | –2.5%
The current factor exposures of Polari do not reflect Boyer's preferred exposures for the next quarter. She considers using a smart beta ETF to implement a tactical allocation.
In Exhibit 2, Boyer compares the characteristics of two smart beta ETFs, zTrak and xShares, both of which track the same US equity market index. Boyer calculates the 3-month holding period cost of investing in the two ETFs.
Exhibit 2
#  | zTrak | xShares
Commission (one-way) | 5 bps | 10 bps
Bid–ask spread on purchase and sale | 15 bps | 10 bps
Annual management fee | 20 bps | 15 bps
As an alternative, Boyer considers investing in yPath, a smart beta exchange-traded note (ETN) issued by a large US investment bank. Boyer compares the structure, creation/redemption mechanism, and counterparty risk of yPath with those of zTrak and xShares.

questions.q: Over the previous quarter, Polari’s investment style has exhibited which of the following?
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because, over the previous quarter, Polari had positive sensitivity to SMB (0.3), which indicates a small-cap, not a large-cap, bias. 
SMB (small minus big) is one of the factors used in Carhart's (1997) four-factor model and is calculated as the average return on three small-cap portfolios minus the average return on three large-cap portfolios. A positive SMB indicates that portfolio returns are driven more by the return on small-cap stocks than by the return on large-cap stocks.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because, over the previous quarter, Polari had a negative sensitivity to WML (–0.1), which indicates a contrarian, not a momentum, bias.
WML (winners minus losers) is one of the factors used in Carhart's (1997) four-factor model and is calculated as the return on a portfolio of the past year’s winners minus the return on a portfolio of the past year’s losers. A negative WML indicates that portfolio returns are driven more by the return of the past year's losers (contrarian bias) than the past year's winners (momentum bias).

questions.q: Over the previous quarter, the active return from security selection for Polari was closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because the return from security selection is calculated as active return minus return from factor sensitivities, instead of factor tilts (i.e., ignoring the return from factor sensitivities of the benchmark).
The return from factor sensitivities is calculated as follows:
RMRF: 1.1 × 5.0% = 5.50%
SMB: 0.3 × (–2.0%) = –0.60%
HML: 0.4 × 1.0% = 0.40%
WML: –0.1 × (–2.5%) = 0.25%
Total return from factor sensitivities = 5.50% – 0.60% + 0.40% + 0.25% = 5.55%
Active return – Return from factor sensitivities = 2.50% – 5.55% = –3.05% ≈ –3.1%
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because this is the total return from factor tilts, not security selection.
The factor tilt return for each of the four factors of the Carhart model is calculated as follows:
RMRF: [(Portfolio sensitivity) − (Benchmark sensitivity)] × (Factor return) = (1.1 – 1.0) × (5.0%) = 0.5%
SMB: [(Portfolio sensitivity) − (Benchmark sensitivity)] × (Factor return) = (0.3 – 0.0) × (–2.0%) = –0.6%
HML: [(Portfolio sensitivity) − (Benchmark sensitivity)] × (Factor return) = (0.4 – 0.2) × (1.0%) = 0.2%
WML: [(Portfolio sensitivity) − (Benchmark sensitivity)] × (Factor return) = (–0.1 – 0.1) × (–2.5%) = 0.5%
Total return from factor tilts = 0.5% – 0.6% + 0.2% + 0.5% = 0.6%
C. Correct.

questions.q: The 3-month holding period cost of investing in the zTrak ETF is:
options: lower than that of the xShares ETF.
the same as that of the xShares ETF.
higher than that of the xShares ETF.
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because zTrak has a lower 3-month holding period cost, however, both ETFs would have the same 12-month holding period cost, calculated as follows:
zTrak: (2 × 5 bps) + 15 bps + 20 bps = 45 bps
xShares: (2 × 10 bps) + 10 bps + 15 bps = 45 bps
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because zTrak has a lower 3-month holding period cost than xShares. If the one-way commission was incorrectly not multiplied by two, this would result in xShares having a lower 3-month holding period cost, calculated as follows:
zTrak: (1 × 5 bps) + 15 bps + (3/12 × 20 bps) = 25 bps
xShares: (1 × 10 bps) + 10 bps + (3/12 × 15 bps) = 23.75 bps

questions.q: Which of the following statements is correct with regard to yPath?
options: Similarly to zTrak and xShares, it holds underlying securities
It has greater potential counterparty risk than zTrak and xShares
Unlike zTrak and xShares, it does not have a creation/redemption mechanism
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because yPath is an ETN and exchange-traded notes (ETNs) are not truly funds because they do not hold underlying securities. ETNs are unsecured debt obligations of the institution that issues them and are structured as a promise to pay a pattern of returns based on the return of the stated index minus fund expenses. The issuer of the note takes responsibility for setting up the counterbalancing hedges it believes necessary to meet the obligations.
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because both ETFs (like zTrak and xShares) and ETNs (like yPath) have creation/redemption mechanisms. ETFs are intrinsically linked to the creation/redemption process, which allows them to operate at lower cost and with greater tax efficiency than mutual funds and generally keeps ETF prices in line with their NAVs. ETNs also "trade on exchanges and have a creation/redemption mechanism.

vignettes.body:
Tina Habba, CFA, provides advisory services to high-net-worth individuals at FundLand, a wealth management firm that distributes both its own funds and third-party funds to clients.
FundLand is setting up a referral fee arrangement with Schula Asset Management. Under this arrangement, Schula provides research services to FundLand in exchange for FundLand distributing Schula's funds. The arrangement has the following characteristics:
Characteristic 1: The estimated value of the research services is $100,000 per year.
Characteristic 2: The research services are provided on an ongoing basis, for as long as FundLand distributes Schula's funds.
Fundland plans to offer a structured note to its clients. The structured note replicates the 1-year return of a US equity index, with a 15% cap on upside return and a maximum loss of 15%. Habba sends a brief email to all of her suitable clients with the following two statements and an invitation to follow up if they require more information:
Statement 1: "This note is attractive because, in my view, the market will trend moderately higher."
Statement 2: "This note provides the return of the US equity index with no downside risk."
Habba receives a call from her client Trey Laurent, who has heard about the structured note. Laurent sends Habba a purchase order for a small amount relative to his total wealth. Laurent's recently updated IPS indicates that the structured note is not suitable for his portfolio. During the call Habba explains to Laurent that the trade is not suitable for him, which he acknowledges. Nonetheless, Laurent insists on purchasing the security. Habba then proceeds to execute the trade order according to his instructions.
Both Habba and FundLand are based in Country A. Habba is preparing to market FundLand’s funds to investors in Country B, a rapidly growing economy. Country B investor protection laws are minimal and there are no restrictions on fund distribution and marketing practices. Country A's laws are more restrictive in this regard than the Standards, but Country A laws state that advisory firms must follow the laws of the local country where they conduct business.

questions.q: To comply with the Standards, which of the characteristics of the referral fee arrangement must Habba disclose to existing and prospective clients?
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because by only disclosing Characteristic 1, Habba would not be disclosing Characteristic 2, which is a required disclosure under the Standards. The disclosure of the referral fee arrangement must include the nature of the consideration or benefit -for example, flat fee or percentage basis, one-time or continuing benefit.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because by only disclosing Characteristic 2, Habba would not be disclosing Characteristic 1, which is a required disclosure under the Standards:
Members and candidates must disclose to clients and prospective clients any benefit received for the recommendation of products or services.
In particular, the disclosure must include the nature of the consideration or benefit together with the estimated dollar value.
C. Correct.

questions.q: In her email regarding the structured note, Habba violates the Standards with:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because Statement 1 states that Habba is basing her recommendation on her view of the market trend, thereby stating that this is her opinion. Standard V(B)–Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients indicates that the content of any investment recommendation should include the distinction between facts and opinions.
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because Statement 1 is not a violation as Habba is, in that statement, stating that the market trend is her opinion and not a fact. Standard V(B)–Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients indicates that the content of any investment recommendation should include the distinction between facts and opinions.

questions.q: Does Habba violate the Standards when executing Laurent's trade order?
options: Yes, because the trade is not suitable for Laurent
Yes, because she should update the IPS before executing the trade
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because, even if the trade is not suitable, Habba should discuss with Laurent that the trade is not suitable for him, with the goal of educating the investor on how the request deviates from the current policy statement, instead of declining the trade outright. Habba does not violate the standards in this respect as she explains to Laurent that the trade is not suitable for him, which he acknowledges.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect, because not updating the IPS is not a violation, given that the trade only accounts for a small amount in relation to Laurent's total wealth: should the unsolicited request be expected to have a material impact on the portfolio, the member or candidate should use this opportunity to update the investment policy statement. Doing so would allow the client to fully understand the potential effect of the requested trade on his or her current goals or risk levels.

questions.q: In marketing the funds in Country B, Habba must follow:
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because, although the case states that Country A's laws are more restrictive in this area than the Standards, Country A's laws state that the laws of the location where business is conducted should govern. In this case, the local laws are laws of Country B which are less strict than the Standards.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because, even if the funds are sold in Country B, the Standards are more restrictive than the laws of Country B, and therefore the Standards should govern instead.

vignettes.body:
Aaron Hardie is an analyst with a commodity trading firm. Hardie is evaluating quantitative models for making predictions in the market for wheat futures.
Hardie models commodity trading positions as he believes they provide information for future price movements. He calculates the net trading position for commercial traders (NTPC) as the difference in the number of long and short contracts as a proportion of the total number of outstanding contracts in week t. Hardie develops two autoregressive (AR) models to help predict the future NTPC:
AR(1) model: NTPCt = 0.003 + 0.949 × NTPCt–1
AR(2) model: NTPCt = 0.003 + 1.096 × NTPCt–1 – 0.116 × NTPCt–2
Hardie uses the models to determine the mean-reverting level of NTPC. He also forecasts NTPC for the next two weeks given that it is 0.061 in the current week and was 0.034 in the prior week. He then uses the regression statistics in Exhibit 1 to compare the forecasting performance of the two models.
Exhibit 1
#  | AR(1) Model | AR(2) Model
R-squared | 0.907 | 0.905
Standard error of regression | 0.027 | 0.027
Root mean squared error | 0.032 | 0.030
Hardie has access to a range of social media and news articles related to agricultural commodity markets. He decides to use this unstructured data to create a sentiment score by classifying articles as positive (Class "1") or negative (Class "0"). Since he plans to use the sentiment score generated by the text classification model to predict market movements, Hardie conducts error analysis on the classifications identified during model training. He uses the confusion matrix shown in Exhibit 2 to calculate the accuracy of the model.
Exhibit 2
# | Actual Class "1" | Actual Class "0"
Predicted Class "1" | 546 | 182
Predicted Class "0" | 140 | 384

questions.q: The mean-reverting level of the AR(1) model is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because the mean-reverting level is mistakenly calculated as b0 / (1 + b1) = 0.003 / (1 + 0.949) = 0.00154 ≈ 0.002.
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because the mean-reverting level is mistakenly calculated as b1 / (1 + b0) = 0.949 / (1 + 0.003) = 0.94616 ≈ 0.946.
This is also closest to swapping the coefficients in the correct calculation: 0.949 / (1 – 0.003) = 0.952.

questions.q: Using the AR(2) model, the 2-week-ahead forecast for NTPC is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because this is the 1-week-ahead forecast of NTPC rather than the 2-week-ahead forecast, calculated as:
xt+1 = b0 + b1xt + b2xt–1 = 0.003 + 1.096 × 0.061 – 0.116 × 0.034 = 0.003 + 0.06686 – 0.00394 = 0.065912 ≈ 0.066.
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because the 2-week-ahead forecast of NTPC is calculated using the chain rule of forecasting but the minus sign for the second lag is mistakenly ignored.
The 1-week-ahead forecast is calculated as xt+1 = b0 + b1xt + b2xt–1 = 0.003 + 1.096 × 0.061 + 0.116 × 0.034 = 0.003 + 0.06686 + 0.00394 = 0.0738
This is then used to forecast xt+2 = b0 + b1xt+1 + b2xt = 0.003 + 1.096 × 0.0738 + 0.116 × 0.061 = 0.003 + 0.08089 + 0.00708 = 0.09096 ≈ 0.091.

questions.q: Compared to the AR(1) model, the out-of-sample forecasting performance of the AR(2) model is:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because we compare the out-of-sample forecasting performance of forecasting models by comparing their root mean squared error (RMSE). The model with the smallest RMSE is judged the most accurate, and not the model with the largest R-squared. This means that the AR(2) model has better out-of-sample forecasting performance.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because we compare the out-of-sample forecasting performance of forecasting models by comparing their root mean squared error (RMSE), and not the standard error of regression. The model with the smallest RMSE is judged the most accurate, which means that the AR(2) model has better out-of-sample forecasting performance.
C. Correct.

questions.q: The accuracy of Hardie's text classification model is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because this is the F1 score of the model, calculated as:
F1 score = (2 × P × R) / (P + R) = (2 × 0.7500 × 0.795918) / (0.7500 + 0.795918) = 1.193878 / 1.545918 = 0.772277 ≈ 0.77,
where
P = Precision = TP / (TP + FP) = 546 / (546 + 182) = 546 / 728 = 0.7500
R = Recall = TP / (TP + FN) = 546 / (546 + 140) = 546 / 686 = 0.795918
and TP = True Positives, FP = False Positives, and FN = False Negatives.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because this is the recall of the model, calculated as:
Recall = TP / (TP + FN) = 546 / (546 + 140) = 546 / 686 = 0.795918 ≈ 0.80,
where TP = True Positives and FN = False Negatives.

vignettes.body:
Olbab Nod is an analyst reviewing economic data from various countries.
Nod begins by calculating the contribution of total factor productivity to economic growth for Country A. He gathers the relevant data in Exhibit 1.
Exhibit 1
Share of capital in GDP | 45.0%
Growth rate of capital | 4.5%
Growth rate of labor | 6.5%
Growth rate of output | 6.7%
Nod observes a consistent increase in Country A's per capita GDP over the past ten years. To better understand this increase, he analyzes the country's labor supply using the information in Exhibit 2.
Exhibit 2
#  | 10 Years Ago | Today
Percentage of population under the age of 16 | 15% | 16%
Percentage of population over the age of 64 | 17% | 19%
Female labor force participation | 50% | 65%
Average hours worked per year | 1,875 | 1,750
Over the next two years, Nod expects an increase in the saving rate in Country A, resulting in increased investment in research and development targeting more efficient production methods. He concludes that this will lead to a permanently higher per capita GDP growth rate in the future, with no diminishing returns to capital.
Nod reviews the information on three developing economies in Exhibit 3. There are no material differences in the countries' saving rates, population growth rates, and production functions. Nod believes that the three countries will benefit from conditional convergence with developed economies.
Exhibit 3
#  | Country B | Country C | Country D
Capital-to-labor ratio | 40% | 40% | 30%
Per capita income | $1,100 | $1,000 | $1,000

questions.q: Based on the growth accounting equation, the growth in total factor productivity in Country A is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because the relative share of capital is used instead of the relative share of labor as follows:
ΔA/A = ΔY/Y – α(ΔK/K) – α(ΔL/L)
ΔA/A = 6.7% – (0.45 × 4.5%) – (0.45 × 6.5%) = 1.75% ≈ 1.8%
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because this is simply the difference between the growth rate of labor (6.5%) and the growth rate of capital (4.5%).

questions.q: The growth in per capita GDP in Country A over the past ten years is best explained by the change in the:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because there has been an increase in the percentage of the population both under the age of 16 and over the age of 64, implying a decrease in the percentage of the population of working age (16–64) compared with ten years ago, which would be contrary to the observed increase in per capita GDP.
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because an increase in the average hours worked typically results in higher output. In this case, the average hours worked per year have decreased, indicating less output and consequently lower per capita GDP.
We can measure the potential size of the labor input as the total number of hours available for work.

questions.q: Nod’s conclusion about Country A’s future per capita GDP growth rate is most consistent with the:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because Nod concludes that the planned significant investments in research and development will result in a permanently higher growth rate in per capita GDP in Country A. This would be inconsistent with the classical growth theory.
Specifically, the classical model predicts that in the long run, the adoption of new technology results in a larger but not richer population. Thus, the standard of living is constant over time even with technological progress, and there is no growth in per capita output.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because Nod concludes that increased investment in research and development will result in a permanently higher growth rate in per capita GDP in Country A, with no diminishing returns to capital. This would be inconsistent with the neoclassical growth theory because it assumes diminishing returns to capital.
Once the economy reaches this steady state, capital deepening cannot be a source of sustained growth in the economy. Only when the economy is operating below the steady state and when the marginal product of capital exceeds its marginal cost can capital deepening raise per capita growth.
C. Correct.

questions.q: Assuming conditional convergence, which country is most likely to experience the highest growth in per capita income?
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because the capital-to-labor ratio for Country B is higher than that for Country D and, as per conditional convergence, the economy with a lower capital-to-labor ratio will experience more rapid growth of productivity and per capita income.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because, even though Country C's per capita income is the same as Country D's, the capital-to-labor ratio for Country C is higher than that for Country D and, as per conditional convergence, the economy with a lower capital-to-labor ratio will experience more rapid growth of productivity and per capita income.
C. Correct.

vignettes.body:
Emily Connelly is an investment analyst at Cove Investment Management. Connelly is analyzing a company that has $250 million in pretax earnings, 40% of which are distributed as dividends while the rest are retained. Both distributed and retained earnings are taxed at a 30% corporate tax rate. Connelly computes the effective tax rate on dividends for a client, Client X, who has a 20% personal tax rate on dividends received.
Connelly evaluates potential stock price reactions to a reduction in dividend payments made by three firms (Firm A, Firm B, and Firm C), based on the metrics shown in Exhibit 1.
Exhibit 1
# Metric | Firm A | Firm B | Firm C
Growth opportunities | High | Low | High
Financial flexibility | High | High | Low
Firm D is a producer of consumer staples and follows a stable dividend policy. Connelly uses the target payout adjustment model to forecast the current year’s dividend based on the information presented in Exhibit 2. She assumes Firm D's dividends will move toward the target payout ratio over four years.
Exhibit 2
Most recent EPS | $3.25
Most recent dividend per share | $1.35
Target payout ratio | 40%
Expected earnings growth rate | 10%
The founder of Firm E owns 51% of the firm's outstanding shares. One of Cove's clients, Client Y, is considering the purchase of all the founder's shares. No other investor holds more than 3% of the outstanding shares. Firm E is located in a country of which the client is not a citizen, and regulations subject foreign ownership holdings in Firm E's equity to 5% voting caps. Connelly considers the ownership structure that would result from this transaction.

questions.q: Client X's effective tax rate on dividends is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because only 40% of pre-tax income is allocated to dividend payments, so only 40% of corporate tax contributes to the effective tax rate on dividends. This answer assumes that the total corporate tax ($75) on pre-tax income contributes to the effective tax rate. It was computed as follows:
Given in vignette:
Pre-tax earnings are $250 million.
Proportion allocated to dividend payments is 40%.
Corporate tax rate is 30%.
Personal tax rate is 20%.
Incorrect solution:
Pre-tax earnings = $250.00
Corporate income tax = 0.30 × $250 = $75
After-tax earnings = $250 – $75 = $175
After-tax earnings paid as dividends = 0.40 × $175 = $70
Shareholder tax on dividends = 0.20 × $70 = $14
Net dividend to shareholders = $70 – $14 = $56
Total taxes paid = $75 + $14 = $89
Effective tax rate on dividends = (Corporate tax + Personal tax) / Pre-tax earnings
Effective tax rate on dividends = $89/$250 = 35.6% ≈ 36%
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because this is simply the sum of the two tax rates; 30% + 20% = 50%. This ignores the fact that dividends are paid from after-tax earnings.

questions.q: Based on Connelly's metrics, the stock price of which firm would most likely have a favorable reaction to a dividend reduction?
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because, while both Firm A and Firm C have high growth opportunities, Firm A has high financial flexibility whereas Firm C does not. Consequently, Firm C would be more likely to have a favorable stock price reaction to a reduction in dividend payments than would Firm A.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because Firm B has low growth opportunities and high financial flexibility. Based on this information, a reduction in dividends by Firm B would most likely result in an unfavorable stock price reaction. Firm B would more likely benefit from an increase in dividend payments.
C. Correct.

questions.q: Based on the approach used by Connelly, Firm D's forecasted dividend per share for the current year is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because this ignores the 'adjustment' component of the forecast model used by Connelly, as follows:
Expected EPS = $3.25 × 1.10 = $3.575
Forecast of dividend per share = $3.575 × 0.40 = $1.43
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because this is computed by assuming that the most recent dividend per share increases at the expected earnings growth rate, as follows:
Forecast of dividend per share = $1.35 × 1.10 = $1.485 ≈ $1.49
Alternatively, this answer can be incorrectly computed as:
Most recent payout ratio = $1.35/$3.25 = 41.54%
Since this payout ratio is above the new, higher target, maintain it for the current year.
Then:
Forecast of dividend per share = $3.25 × 1.10 × 41.54% = $1.485 ≈ $1.49

questions.q: The ownership structure that would result from the Firm E transaction is best characterized as having:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because Client Y will own 51% of Firm E shares, giving the client concentrated ownership. The voting caps will prevent the client from having concentrated control.
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because, while Client Y will have concentrated ownership (51% of shares), the voting caps on foreign investors in Firm E will prevent concentrated control.

vignettes.body:
Karl Reinke, a research analyst, is examining the financial statements of Argon plc, a UK-based company that reports under IFRS. Argon's primary competitors are US-based companies that report under US GAAP. On 1 January of the current year, Argon purchased a 40% non-controlling interest in Xenon plc for GBP 500 million. The book values of the assets and liabilities were equal to their fair values except for inventory, which was undervalued by GBP 5 million, and equipment, which was undervalued by GBP 10 million. Xenon uses the FIFO inventory valuation method and depreciates all of its equipment using the straight-line method. The equipment has an estimated remaining useful life of ten years with no residual value. Reinke estimates that Xenon will report net income of GBP 60 million and will not declare any dividends for the current year.
Argon also acquired an 80% controlling interest in Radon plc in the current year, and has elected to use the partial goodwill option for recognizing goodwill when consolidating Radon.
Reinke next examines Argon's financial statement trends for the past three reported years. He compiles the accruals ratios in Exhibit 1, and the Beneish M-scores and Altman Z-scores in Exhibit 2.
Exhibit 1
# | Most Recent Year | Two Years Ago | Three Years Ago
Cash-flow-based accruals ratio | –3.6% | –2.4% | 1.1%
Balance-sheet-based accruals ratio | 2.5% | –2.9% | –4.4%
Exhibit 2
# | Most Recent Year | Two Years Ago | Three Years Ago
Beneish M-score | –1.93 | –1.81 | –1.76
Altman Z-score | 3.03 | 2.86 | 2.78

questions.q: The estimated amount of Argon's investment in Xenon at the end of the current year should be:
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because the depreciation for the undervalued equipment is treated as though it was overvalued (500.0 + 24.0 – 2.0 + 0.4 = 522.4).
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because the deduction for the inventory sold under the FIFO valuation method is omitted from the calculation (500.0 + 24.0 – 0.4 = 523.6).

questions.q: When consolidating Radon, Argon's D/E ratio at the end of the current year would be:
options: lower than if it used the method of its primary competitors.
the same as if it used the method of its primary competitors.
higher than if it used the method of its primary competitors.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because total shareholders' equity is lower under the partial goodwill method, thereby increasing the debt-to-equity ratio. Total debt is the same under both methods.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because total shareholders' equity is lower under the partial goodwill method, thereby increasing the debt-to-equity ratio. Total debt is the same under both methods. 
C. Correct.

questions.q: With respect to the trends in the cash-flow-based and the balance-sheet-based accruals ratios, Reinke should conclude that:
options: only the cash-flow-based accruals ratio has improved.
only the balance-sheet-based-accruals ratio has improved.
both the cash-flow-based and the balance-sheet-based accruals ratios have improved.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because the absolute values of the cash-flow-based accruals ratio have trended further away from zero. This is a deteriorating trend.
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because, while the balance-sheet-based accruals ratio has improved, the absolute values of the cash-flow-based accruals ratios have trended further away from zero. This is a deteriorating trend.

questions.q: Regarding the trends in the Altman Z-score and the Beneish M-score, Reinke should conclude that:
options: only the Altman Z-score has improved.
only the Beneish M-score has improved.
both the Altman Z-score and the Beneish M-score have improved.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because the Beneish M-score has also improved.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because the Altman Z-score has also improved.
C. Correct.

sets.title: Mock F · Paper 2
sets.desc: Real CFA Institute Level II Mock 4, Session 2: vignettes, questions and explanations as published (44 questions, 2 h 12 min).

vignettes.body:
Tokushi Stone is a risk manager at Brockway Asset Management, a multi-manager hedge fund. Brockway has $10 billion in assets under management across three strategies: equity long–short, quantitative, and fixed income.
Brockway's entity-level risk exposure is measured and monitored using VaR. Stone prepares a quarterly risk report and determines that the entity-level daily VaR is $15.8 million at the 95% confidence level.
Stone first evaluates Brockway's equity long–short strategy. To calculate the VaR of the equity long–short portfolio, Stone compiles the portfolio characteristics in Exhibit 1 and estimates the monthly VaR at the 95% confidence level using the variance–covariance method. At the 95% confidence level, the critical value of the one-tailed z-statistic is 1.65.
Exhibit 1
Expected monthly return | 0.738%
Monthly volatility of returns | 1.100%
Portfolio value | $500 million
Next, Stone reviews backtesting results of two portfolios for Brockway's quantitative strategy. Summary statistics using monthly returns for the two portfolios are presented in Exhibit 2.
Exhibit 2
#  | Portfolio 1 | Portfolio 2
Mean return | 0.7% | 0.6%
Standard deviation | 1.5% | 0.8%
Skewness | –1.9 | 1.1
Kurtosis | 15.8 | 4.6
VaR (95%) | –1.9% | –0.6%
Conditional VaR (95%) | –6.9% | –2.3%
Finally, Stone reviews Brockway's fixed-income strategy, which uses a multifactor model to pick undervalued securities. He estimates downside risk measures for the strategy using Monte Carlo simulation. To perform the simulation, Stone specifies a functional form using ten factors and calibrates the model to a multivariate Student’s t-distribution. The model is complex and several factors have limited historical data.

questions.q: Based on the measure included in the quarterly report, Stone should expect Brockway to lose:
options: at least $15.8 million in a day 5% of the time.
on average $15.8 million in a day 5% of the time.
at most $15.8 million in a day 5% of the time.
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because $15.8 million is the minimum loss in a day and not the average loss that the fund would expect to experience. These are the explicit elements of a VaR statement: the frequency of losses of a given minimum magnitude expressed either in currency or percentage terms.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because VaR is the minimum and not the maximum loss that would be expected a certain percentage of the time over a specified period of time, given the assumed market conditions. As per the vignette, Brockway should expect to lose at least $15.8 million in a day 5% of the time.

questions.q: The monthly VaR of the equity long–short portfolio at the 95% confidence level is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because the calculation omits the z-value of 1.65.
VaR = [E(Rp) – σp](–1)(Portfolio Value)
The monthly 5% VaR is incorrectly calculated as:
[0.738% – 1.100%](–1)($500,000,000) = $1,810,000 ≈ $1.8 million
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because the expected return is omitted in the equation for VaR and only volatility is taken into consideration:
VaR = 1.65σp(Portfolio Value)
The monthly 5% VaR is incorrectly calculated as:
[1.65 × 1.100%] × $500,000,000 = $9,075,000 ≈ $9.1 million

questions.q: Based on the backtesting results, Portfolio 1 has a:
options: lower volatility of returns than Portfolio 2.
smaller expected tail loss than Portfolio 2.
higher probability of large negative returns than Portfolio 2.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because Portfolio 1 has a higher standard deviation of returns (1.5%) than Portfolio 2 (0.8%).
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because Portfolio 1 has a larger expected tail loss as measured by CVaR (the average loss conditional on exceeding the VaR cutoff). Portfolio 1 has a CVaR of –6.9% and Portfolio 2 has a CVaR of –2.3%.
C. Correct.

questions.q: The model used in Stone’s Monte Carlo simulation most likely has a:
options: low probability of producing extreme return estimates.
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because high specification error arises when the model is overly simplistic.
Overly simplistic models require fewer parameters (therefore, they might have low estimation errors), but they may not fit the data well (because they are mis-specified). Stone’s model is complex and has ten key decision variables.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because a multivariate Student’s t-distribution is used, which has fatter tails than the normal distribution and accounts for a higher probability of extreme events. The Student’s t-distribution is a natural extension of the multivariate normal distribution, because it has the ability to account for the skewness and the excess kurtosis often observed in factor and asset return data. Excess kurtosis indicates a higher probability of extreme events.

vignettes.body:
Chun Tian is a US-based portfolio manager actively involved in the foreign exchange market.
Three months ago, Tian made a 6-month deposit of 50 million Australian dollars (AUD) at the annualized 6-month AUD reference interest rate. She then fully hedged the deposit by selling AUD forward against USD. Today, she marks the forward position to market and notes that reference rates have not changed over the past three months. Selected current reference rates are provided in Exhibit 1.
Exhibit 1
#  | 3-Month | 6-Month
AUD reference rate (annualized) | 0.60% | 0.67%
USD reference rate (annualized) | 0.26% | 0.36%
Next, Tian researches Cambodia, an emerging market that has the riel (KHR) as its currency. Tian notes that the 1-year KHR reference rate is 1.50% and the 1-year USD reference rate is 0.67%. The current KHR/USD (number of KHR per USD) spot rate is 4,100.00 and Tian expects the spot rate to be 4,161.50 one year from now. Tian explores a potential carry trade based on this information.
One week later, Tian determines whether a triangular arbitrage opportunity exists based on the dealer quotes provided in Exhibit 2.

Yes, by buying KHR from Dealer 2 and selling it to Dealer 1

B. Incorrect. Incorrect because buying KHR from Dealer 1 is more expensive than buying KHR from Dealer 2. Doing this transaction would imply buying KHR at 0.0266 JPY and selling at 0.0250 JPY, thereby making a loss for every KHR bought and sold.

questions.q: Based on Tian's conclusion and the Mundell–Fleming model, Country L's currency will most likely:

A. Incorrect. Incorrect.
