vignettes.body:
Fabiano Arlandi, a portfolio manager, is analyzing the term structure of credit spreads for three companies.
Company A is a high-quality issuer with a strong competitive position in a stable industry with strong fundamentals; the company is currently refinancing near-term maturities with long-term debt.
Company B was recently acquired in a leveraged buyout by an experienced team that is expected to restructure the organization and improve margins and profitability.
Company C operates in a cyclical industry that is currently at the bottom of its economic cycle.
Arlandi determines the credit spread of Company A's zero-coupon bond over a default-risk-free government bond, given the following information:
The bond has a remaining maturity of five years and a face value of 100.
The default-risk-free discount rate is 4% and the government yield curve is flat.
The credit valuation adjustment is 2.924.
Arlandi assumes there is no interest rate volatility.
Three months ago, Arlandi bought $10 million of 5-year protection on Company B through a CDS contract with a duration of 3.7 years. The CDS credit spread has since narrowed from 350 bps to 220 bps currently. Arlandi closes out the trade by selling the CDS contract.
Arlandi purchases CDS protection on a 7-year senior unsecured bond issued by Company C and held in his portfolio. Several months after purchasing protection, a credit event occurs. The following bonds of Company C are trading in the market.
Bond 1: 7-year subordinated unsecured bond trading at 25% of par
Bond 2: 3-year senior unsecured bond trading at 35% of par
Bond 3: 7-year senior unsecured bond trading at 45% of par

questions.q: The term structure of credit spreads is most likely upward sloping for:
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because an inverted credit spread curve is typical for a company undergoing a leveraged buyout. For example, an ownership change resulting from a leveraged buyout or private equity acquisition may often be accompanied by a significant increase of leverage. In such a case, an inverted credit curve may indicate investor expectations that the new owners will create efficiencies in the restructured organization, leading to improved future cash flows and profitability that will benefit debt investors.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because an inverted credit spread curve is typical for a company at the bottom of the economic cycle. Another example of an inverted credit term structure might result when issuers in a historically cyclical industry (such as oil and gas exploration or retail) find themselves at the bottom of an economic cycle, with investor expectations of a recovery in the industry tied to improving credit spreads over time.

questions.q: The credit spread for Company A's zero-coupon bond is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because the credit valuation adjustment is divided by 5. 
(1) The present value of the default-risk-free bond is 100/1.045 = 82.1927
(2) Incorrectly subtracting only 1/5 of the credit valuation adjustment yields 82.1927 – 2.924/5 = 81.6079
(3) Hence the yield on the corporate bond is calculated as (100/81.6079)0.2 – 1 = 4.149%
(4) Subtracting the default-risk-free discount rate of 4%: 4.149% – 4% = 0.149% ≈ 0.15%
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because the credit valuation adjustment is added to the present value of the default-risk-free bond, rather than subtracted, and the resulting yield is subtracted from the 4% risk-free yield—not the reverse. 
(1) The present value of the corresponding risk-free bond is 100/1.045 = 82.1927
(2) Incorrectly adding the credit valuation adjustment yields 82.1927 + 2.924 = 85.1167
(3) Hence the yield on the corporate bond is calculated as (100/85.1167)0.2 – 1 = 3.2754%
(4) Subtracting this value from 4.00% yields 4% – 3.2754% = 0.7246% ≈ 0.72%
C. Correct.

questions.q: The estimated loss on the CDS trade on Company B is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because the term to maturity of 5 years is used instead of duration:
Estimated loss = Change in credit spread × Term to maturity × Notional amount
= (220 bps – 350 bps) × 5.0 × $10 million = –130 bps × 5.0 × $10 million = –$650,000.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because the negative ending spread of 220 bps is used instead of the change in the spread: 
Estimated loss = –Ending credit spread × Duration × Notional amount
= –220 bps × 3.7 × $10 million = –220 bps × 3.7 × $10 million = –$814,000.

questions.q: The cheapest-to-deliver obligation for the CDS contract on the Company C senior unsecured bond is:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because Bond 1 is subordinated and therefore does not qualify as the cheapest-to-deliver obligation under the CDS. 
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because Bond 3 is priced higher than Bond 2. The two bonds are of the same seniority and therefore the payoff of the CDS is determined by the cheapest-to-deliver obligation.

vignettes.body:
Yasmine Bernal, an equity analyst, is valuing two port operators: Ariel Port Inc and Boston Terminals Ltd. Bernal uses [free cash flow models] to value the stocks.
Ariel Port is an established business, which maintains moderate leverage and has steadily growing cash flows. Boston Terminals is completing construction of its second terminal this year, partially financed with new debt. Bernal forecasts that revenues of Boston Terminals will rise significantly in the first two years of operations of the new terminal and then stabilize. Bernal expects the leverage of Boston Terminals to decrease in the medium term once the second terminal is operational and the new debt is gradually repaid.
Ariel Port
Bernal reviews key financial data from Ariel Port, which reports under IFRS. Based on data from Ariel's annual report in Exhibit 1, Bernal gathers data for the latest reporting year starting from cash flow from operations (CFO). Ariel Port's tax rate is 30%.
Exhibit 1
Cash Flow Statement ($ Million)
Net income | 648.2
Depreciation and amortization | 900.0
Decrease/(increase) in working capital | 100.0
Interest expense | 183.4
Cash flow from operations | 1,831.6
Net purchases of fixed assets | (370.0)
Cash flow from investing activities | (370.0)
New borrowings | 2,298.0
Repayment of borrowings | (1,944.0)
Interest expense | (262.0)
Cash flow from financing activities | 92.0
Net change in cash | 1,553.6
Boston Terminals
Bernal reviews Boston Terminals fundamental data and identifies three variables to consider:
Variable 1: The dividend payout ratio will decrease in the future
Variable 2: Boston Terminals will have an inconsistent capital structure
Variable 3: Capital expenditures will increase dramatically
Bernal decides to use FCFF to value Boston Terminals.
There are rumors that Boston Terminals plans to acquire a competitor, whose shares are currently trading at $24.1 per share. Bernal would like to determine if the stock is fairly valued, using the following assumptions:
FCFF is estimated at $368 million in Year 1, $442 million in Year 2 and is expected to grow by 3% per year afterwards.
WACC is 12% and number of outstanding shares is 100 million.
Market value of non-operating assets is $300 million.
Book value of debt is $2,000 million and market value of debt is $2,300 million.
Bernal thinks that the competitor is likely to deploy anti-takeover measures against acquisition by Boston Terminals. She believes the competitor will issue new debt and use the proceeds to buy-back its own shares. Bernal assesses how these measures will affect the competitor's FCFF and FCFE.

questions.q: Which approach is the most appropriate to value equity of the stocks Bernel is analyzing?
options: FCFE for both Ariel Ports and Boston Terminals
FCFE for Boston Terminals and FCFF for Ariel Ports
FCFE for Ariel Ports and FCFF for Boston Terminals
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because FCFF should be used for Boston Terminals. FCFF estimation is easier than FCFE estimation when the firm's leverage is changing. FCFE is less appropriate to value the equity of Boston Terminals than FCFF due to its changing capital structure. Boston Terminal's capital structure is changing and amounts of borrowings will be fluctuating in the medium-term. Therefore, FCFF will be more appropriate to use. Also, the required return on equity might be expected to be more sensitive to changes in financial leverage than changes in the WACC, making the use of a constant discount rate difficult to justify.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because FCFF should be used for Boston Terminals and FCFE should be used for Ariel Ports.
FCFF estimation is easier than FCFE estimation when the firm's leverage is changing. Large swings in net borrowings will cause large changes in FCFE and interest expense. In addition, the required return on equity might be expected to be more sensitive to changes in financial leverage than changes in the WACC, making the use of a constant discount rate difficult to justify. Boston Terminal's capital structure is changing and amounts of borrowings will be fluctuating in the medium-term. Therefore, FCFF will be more appropriate to use.
An analyst may prefer to use one approach rather than the other because of the characteristics of the company being valued. For example, if the company's structure is relatively stable, using FCFE to value equity is more direct and simpler than using FCFF. Ariel Ports is an established business with steadily growing cash flows and a capital structure that is stable. I.e. it maintains a moderate leverage. Therefore, the use of FCFE is preferred.
C. Correct.

questions.q: Ariel Port's FCFF is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because in the FCFF calculation, interest expense is mistakenly added back to cash flow from operations and as a result is double counted.
The incorrect calculation of FCFF is thus:
FCFF = CFO + Interest Expense (1-Tax rate) - CFInv
FCFF = 1,831.6 + 262*(1-30%) - 370 = $1,645 million
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because this is the FCFE equation which adds net borrowing.
Net borrowing is calculated as: new borrowings - repayment of borrowings = 2,298.0 - 1,944.0 = 354
FCFE = CFO - FCInv + Net borrowing = 1,831.6 - 370 + 354 = $1,815.6 million

questions.q: Based on her assumptions for Boston Terminals competitor, Bernal should conclude that the stock is:
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because the fair value of the Boston Terminals competitor is $27.1 per share whereas the shares are currently trading at $24.1 per share. The correct calculation of equity value = Value of operating assets + MV of non-operating assets - MV of debt. However, if the MV of non-operating assets is mistakenly omitted from the formula, this will lead to: 
Equity value = Value of operating assets - MV of debt
Equity value = 4,709.5 - 2,300 = 2,409.5
Share price = $2,409.5 million/100 million shares = $24.1.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because the fair value of the Boston Terminals competitor is $27.1 per share whereas the shares are currently trading at $24.1 per share. The correct calculation of equity value = Value of operating assets + MV of non-operating assets - MV of debt. However, if book value of debt is mistakenly used instead of MV of debt, this will lead to: 
Equity value = Value of operating assets + Value of non-operating assets - Book Value of debt
Equity value = 4,709.5 + 300 - 2,000 = 3,009.5
Share price = $3,009.5 million/100 million shares = $30.1.

questions.q: The competitor's anti-takeover measures against the acquisition by Boston Terminals will:
options: not impact FCFF and increase FCFE.
not impact FCFF and decrease FCFE.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because an increase in debt and share buy-backs are cash flows available to all investors, including shareholders, and as a result have no effect on FCFF. An increase in net borrowings increases FCFE in the year of issuance.
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because an increase in debt and share buy-backs are cash flows available to all investors, including shareholders, and as a result have no effect on FCFF. An increase in net borrowings increases FCFE in the year of issuance.

vignettes.body:
Susan Li, CFA, an equity research analyst with Maipo Canyon Investment Bank (MCIB), specializes in identifying companies that are likely takeover candidates. MCIB has adopted the Standards as part of its ethics and compliance policy.
Bloomberry, an institutional client of MCIB, recently earned a substantial return on a stock recommended by Li. To show its appreciation, Bloomberry offers Li tickets to a sold-out Broadway show as a gift. Li accepts the gift and plans to take her family to the show. Li does not notify her supervisor that she accepted the gift.
In a recently published investment report, Li included a table with statistical analysis of publicly available information from a well-recognized industry journal. By downloading the table and not performing the statistical analysis herself, she saved considerable time and effort. Li did not cite the source of the table in her report nor did she verify the statistical analysis.
Li uses MCIB's proprietary model to identify companies that are likely takeover candidates. The proprietary model uses third-party accounting data. Although Li lacks the relevant programming skills, she understands the assumptions and limitations of the proprietary model. Li does not verify the underlying third-party data herself because MCIB has an established procedure for verifying the data.
MCIB's proprietary model predicts that a takeover of Godoggo Corporation is highly likely. In a recent report, Li assigned a "Buy" recommendation to Godoggo's stock. Based on the report, one of MCIB's portfolio managers buys a large number of shares in Godoggo for his fund. He subsequently promotes the stock in several online chat rooms by stating, "I have purchased Godoggo stock because our internal research indicates that it is highly likely to be taken over." A week later, the price of Godoggo's stock has doubled and the portfolio manager subsequently sells all the shares of the stock in his fund.

questions.q: Do Li's actions regarding the tickets violate the Standard relating to independence and objectivity?
options: Yes, because Li should have refused the tickets
Yes, because Li should have notified her supervisor
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because Li did not disclose the gift from the client to her employer.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because Li does not have to refuse the tickets in order to be consistent with Standard I(B) - Independence and Objectivity, but she does have to disclose the gift to her employer. Members may accept gifts from clients as long as they disclose them to their employer because gifts in a client relationship are deemed less likely to affect a member's objectivity and independence than gifts in other situations.
C. Correct.

questions.q: By including the table in her investment report, did Li violate the Standard relating to misrepresentation?
options: Yes, by not citing the source
Yes, by not verifying the statistical analysis
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because Li committed plagiarism by mispresenting the statistical analysis in the table as her own work.
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because failing to verify the statistical analysis is not a violation of Standard I(C) - Misrepresentation. Because the statistical analysis table is from a reputable source (a well-recognized industry journal), under Standard V(A) - Diligence and Reasonable Basis, it can reasonably be relied upon without Li having to verify the analysis for herself.
When providing information to clients from a third party, members and candidates share a responsibility for the accuracy of the marketing and distribution materials that pertain to the third party’s capabilities, services, and products.

questions.q: By using MCIB's proprietary model in her analysis, does Li violate the Standard relating to diligence and reasonable basis?
options: Yes, because she lacks the relevant programming skills
Yes, because she does not verify the third-party data used in the model
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because Li is not required to become an expert in every technical aspect of the proprietary model. It is sufficient for her to understand the assumptions and limitations of the model.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because Li's firm has a procedure for verifying third-party information. Standard V(A) - Diligence and Reasonable Basis does not require verification of the data by Li.

questions.q: Are the portfolio manager's actions with regard to Godoggo shares a violation of the Standard relating to market manipulation?
options: Yes, because he engaged in transaction-based market manipulation
Yes, because he engaged in information-based market manipulation
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because the manager bought the stock based on a recommendation in Li's report and presumably sold the stock because its price had doubled.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because the portfolio manager's promotion of the stock was based on a recommendation contained in a report. The portfolio manager was not seemingly attempting to spread false information about the stock.

vignettes.body:
Joanne Gordon is a buy-side analyst covering the banking and insurance sectors.
Gordon first analyzes the liquidity of Grand Bank. She reviews the information (in $ millions) from the bank's most recent annual report in Exhibit 1 and calculates its liquidity coverage ratio.
Exhibit 1
High-quality liquid assets | 400
Net cash outflows | 300
High-quality liquid assets in excess of net cash outflows | 100
Total available stable funding | 1,300
Total required stable funding | 1,100
Gordon next evaluates the performance of a property and casualty insurance company, Bronx Insurance Company. She calculates the company's combined ratio for the most recent year using the information (in $ millions) presented in Exhibit 2.
Exhibit 2
Net premiums written | 3,600
Net premiums earned | 3,200
Loss and loss adjustment expenses | 2,300
Underwriting expenses | 990
Dividends paid to policyholders | 100
Bronx Insurance has two share-based compensation plans: (1) a restricted stock unit (RSU) plan for employees; and (2) executive stock options. Settlement for the RSUs is made at the end of each year. On the grant date at the beginning of the first year, the share price was $6.00 per RSU. At the end of the second year, the share price was $5.00 per RSU. The CEO has vested stock options equivalent to 10% of the company's current outstanding shares. Gordon forecasts a net loss for Bronx Insurance during the second year of the RSU plan.

questions.q: The liquidity coverage ratio for Grand Bank is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because the calculation uses the high-quality liquid assets (HQLA) in excess of net cash outflows in the numerator instead of total high-quality liquid assets as required.
LCR = HQLA in excess of net cash outflows/Net cash outflows = 100/300 ≈ 33%
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because this is the value for the net stable funding ratio. 
Net stable funding ratio = Total available stable funding/Total required stable funding
= 1,300/1,100 ≈ 118%
C. Correct.

questions.q: The combined ratio for Bronx Insurance is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because this calculation uses net premiums written, rather than net premiums earned as the denominator of the loss and loss adjustment expense ratio:
Loss and loss adjustment expense ratio = Loss and loss adjustment expenses/Net premiums earned = 2,300/3,600 ≈ 63.9%
Underwriting expense ratio = Underwriting expenses/Net premiums written = 990/3,600 = 27.5%
Combined ratio = 63.9% + 27.5% = 91.4% ≈ 91%
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because it is the combined ratio after dividends, rather than the combined ratio.
The combined ratio after dividends is calculated as the combined ratio plus the dividends to policyholders ratio.
Dividends to policyholders ratio = Dividends paid to policyholders/Net premiums earned = 100/3,200 ≈ 3.1%
Combined ratio after dividends = 99.4% + 3.1% = 102.5% ≈ 103%

questions.q: During the second year of the RSU plan, Bronx Insurance incurred:
options: neither a tax shortfall nor an excess tax benefit.
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because the share price of $5.00 on the settlement date at the end of the second year is lower than the share price of $6.00 on the grant date, resulting in a tax shortfall.
A higher share price at settlement versus the grant date results in a higher tax deduction than the cumulative stock-based compensation expense. This is known as an excess tax benefit or tax windfall because taxable income and tax expense are reduced.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because the share price of $5.00 on the settlement date at the end of the second year is lower than the share price of $6.00 on the grant date, resulting in a tax shortfall.

questions.q: As a result of the employee RSU plan and executive stock options, Gordon's forecasted value for diluted EPS of the second year of the RSU plan should be:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because when EPS is positive, unvested RSUs are added to shares outstanding balance, resulting in a lower diluted EPS than basic EPS. The options would be excluded from the calculation as they are anti-dilutive: exercise is uneconomic for the holder, and if they were exercised, fewer shares would be issued upon their exercise than would be repurchased with the resulting cash received, reducing shares outstanding and increasing EPS.
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because diluted EPS cannot exceed basic EPS, so companies that report a net loss will report the same basic and diluted shares outstanding.

vignettes.body:
Elaine Azul is an investment advisor at a mid-sized US investment firm. She is preparing for meetings with two of her clients, Jacob Green and Stella White.
Jacob Green has a large position in the non-dividend-paying stock of his own firm. Four months ago, Azul advised Green to reduce his exposure to the firm's stock by $2 million. Due to tax considerations, Green entered into a short 6-month equity forward contract for the firm's stock instead of selling the shares outright. At the meeting, Green asks Azul how the value of the current forward position would be affected if the company pays a $3.50 dividend in three months and the share price is unchanged.

Azul is evaluating longer-term solutions to reduce Green’s exposure to the firm’s stock. One approach is to enter into a 3-year equity swap. The proposed equity swap has a semiannual reset, a 30/360 day count, a 2.5% annual fixed rate, and a $2 million notional principal.

Azul's second client, Stella White, is expecting a cash inflow of $5 million in three months that she plans to deposit for six months in a non-domestic account. Azul suggests protecting this investment from an expected decrease in interest rates. She proposes a market reference rate (MRR)-based 3 × 9 forward rate agreement (FRA) that is advanced set, advanced settled. Relevant MRR data are presented in Exhibit 1.

Exhibit 1
# Maturity | MRR Spot Rate (Annualized)
3 months | 0.72%
6 months | 0.93%
9 months | 1.20%
Two years ago, White entered into a local market $7 million 5-year interest rate swap with annual resets (30/360 day count), receiving the fixed rate of 1.36% and paying the MRR. Azul determines the value of the swap today using the relevant spot rate data in Exhibit 2.

Exhibit 2
# Maturity | Spot Rate | Present Value Factor
1 year | 0.262% | 0.9974
2 years | 0.672% | 0.9867
3 years | 0.956% | 0.9721
4 years | 1.140% | 0.9564
5 years | 1.280% | 0.9398

questions.q: Azul's best response to Green’s question regarding the value of the forward position is that it will:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because the dividend is paid after the forward contract expires, therefore there is no impact on the value of the forward contract. If the dividend did occur before the forward contract expired, this answer would still be incorrect because Green shorted the forward and the payment of a dividend would increase the value of his position. However, in case of a long position, the value of his position would decrease.
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because the dividend is paid after the forward contract expires. However, if the dividend did occur before the forward contract expired, this answer would be correct because Green shorted the forward and the payment of a dividend would increase the value of his position.

questions.q: If Green's stock has a –4.5% return (not annualized) over the next six months, the proposed equity swap's net cash flow to Green on its first payment date would be:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because Green would receive fixed and pay the equity return. If the negative equity return is considered an outflow, this coupled with the receipt of the fixed payment would result in a negative cash flow of –$65,000:
Receive Fixed Cash Flow = 0.025/2 × $2 million = $25,000
Pay Equity Cash Flow = –0.045 × $2 million = –$90,000
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because the cash inflow from the fixed-rate receipt is not adjusted for a semi-annual reset; –$2,000,000 × (0.025 – (–0.045)) = $140,000.

questions.q: The fixed rate on the 3 × 9 FRA is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because the calculation assumes m = the term of the deposit, 270 days instead of 180 days.
FRA0= {[1 + (0.0120 × (270/360))]/[1 + (0.0072 × (90/360))] – 1}/(270/360) = 0.9583%
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because the calculation uses the 6-month rate, 0.93%, instead of the 9-month rate, 1.20%.
FRA0 = {[1 + (0.0093 × (270/360))]/[1 + (0.0072 × (90/360))] – 1}/(180/360) = 1.0331%
C. Correct.

questions.q: The current value of White’s interest rate swap is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because the calculation of the current fixed swap rate uses the sum of the FV factors based on spot rates in years 3, 4, and 5 (2.8683). This yields a FSt of 2.10%.
FSt = (1 – 0.9398)/2.8683 = 0.020988.
Value of Swap = $7 million × (0.0136 – 0.020988) × 2.8683 = –$148,338.
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because the current fixed swap rate (FSt) is calculated as the average of the spot rates in year 1, 2, and 3 (0.63%).
Value of Swap = $7 million × (0.0136 – 0.0063) × 2.9562 = $151,062.

vignettes.body:
Chloe Smith is an equity analyst evaluating Calpurnia Corp., a multinational company based in the US. Calpurnia reports under US GAAP and its fiscal year end is 31 December. Its reporting currency is the USD.
Calpurnia has certain transactions in EUR and also has foreign subsidiaries which report in EUR. Smith analyzes the effect of these on Calpurnia's consolidated financial statements. The USD/EUR (number of USD per 1 EUR) exchange rates over the most recent year are in Exhibit 1.
Exhibit 1
#  | USD/EUR
1 January | 1.14
15 December | 1.08
31 December | 1.05
Average for the year | 1.10
On 15 December of the most recent year, Calpurnia purchased inventory from a supplier in Spain for EUR 50 million. Calpurnia paid for the inventory on 31 January of the current year.
On 1 January of the most recent year, Calpurnia established a wholly-owned subsidiary in the Eurozone, Bartolo AG. Bartolo has the EUR as its reporting currency and uses the FIFO method to account for inventory. The exchange rate when Bartolo's inventory was purchased over the most recent year was 1.11. Bartolo's financial statements are translated into USD using the current rate method. Smith considers the effect of translation on Bartolo's gross profit margin. For the most recent year, Bartolo reported net income of EUR 10 million. On 15 December, Bartolo declared dividends of EUR 800,000.
Finally, Smith evaluates the sustainability of growth in Calpurnia's geographic segments. She gathers information on the components of total net sales growth in Exhibit 2.
Exhibit 2
# Geographic Segment | Contribution from Volume Growth | Contribution from Price Growth | Contribution from Foreign Currency Exchange | Total Net Sales Growth
Eurozone | 9.3% | 4.5% | –2.5% | 11.3%
Americas | 10.1% | 2.4% | 0.6% | 13.1%
Asia Pacific | 8.1% | 0.4% | 5.4% | 13.9%

questions.q: For the most recent year, Calpurnia's inventory purchase resulted in a foreign exchange:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because the foreign exchange transaction effect is calculated as the difference between the value using the exchange rate at 31 December of the most recent year and value at the date of purchase (cost) rather than vice versa as follows:
Inventory cost in USD at purchase date: EUR 50 million × 1.08 = USD 54 million.
Inventory cost in USD at 31 December of the most recent year = EUR 50 million × 1.05 = USD 52.5 million
FX Gain (Loss) (incorrect) = USD 52.5 million - USD 54 million = (USD 1.5 million)
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because the foreign exchange transaction effect is calculated using the most recent year average USD/EUR exchange rate of 1.10 instead of the USD/EUR exchange rate of 1.05 at 31 December of the most recent year as follows:
Inventory cost in USD at purchase date = EUR 50 million × 1.08 = USD 54 million.
Inventory cost in USD at average rate = EUR 50 million × 1.10 = USD 55 million
FX Gain (Loss) = USD 54 million - USD 55 million = (USD 1 million)
C. Correct.

questions.q: After Bartolo’s financial statements are translated into USD, its gross profit margin would be:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because under the current rate method, sales and cost of goods sold must be translated using the same rate (average rate during the year). Gross profit margin does not change in translation.
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because under the current method both sales and cost of goods sold must be translated using the same rate (the average rate for the most recent year). Gross profit margin does not change in translation.

questions.q: The increase in Bartolo's retained earnings when translated into USD for the most recent year is:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because the increase in retained earnings is translated using the current rate as of the end of the most recent year:
Net increase in retained earnings (incorrect): (EUR 10,000,000 – EUR 800,000) × 1.05 = USD 9,660,000.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because the increase in Bartolo's retained earnings is translated by using the average rate of the most recent year as follows:
Increase in retained earnings: (EUR 10,000,000 – EUR 800,000) × 1.10 = USD 10,120,000.
C. Correct.

questions.q: Based on the components of total net sales growth, which of Calpurnia's segments has the highest sustainable growth rate?
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because the Americas segment, while having the highest Contribution from Volume growth, has a combined sustainable volume and price growth component of only 12.5% (10.1% + 2.4%), which is lower than the sustainable component of growth in the Eurozone (13.8%). In addition, it has a contribution for foreign currency exchange (0.6%) that is higher than that of the Eurozone (–2.5%), which also points to a less sustainable overall growth than that of the Eurozone.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because the Asia Pacific segment, while having the highest Total Net Sales Growth rate at 13.9%, has only 8.5% of that growth due to the combined effect of volume and price, which represents the sustainable component of growth. The remaining 5.4% is due to currency fluctuations, which are outside the control of Calpurnia's management. The sustainable component of growth in Asia Pacific (8.5%) is lower than the sustainable component of growth in the Eurozone (13.8%). In addition, the Asia Pacific segment has a contribution for foreign currency exchange (5.4%) that is higher than that of the Eurozone (–2.5%), which also points to a less sustainable overall growth than that of the Eurozone.

vignettes.body:
Sarah Kendall is an analyst at a commodity trading firm. She is tasked with evaluating quantitative models to explain precious metal returns. Kendall develops a model with three factors to explain weekly returns (RET):
RETt = b0 + b1FSIt + b2EPUt + b3GPRt + εt,
where FSI is the weekly change in the financial stress index, EPU is the weekly change in economic policy uncertainty, and GPR is the weekly change in geopolitical risk. She estimates the model for silver and platinum returns using 624 weekly observations.
Kendall gathers the model output for silver returns and tests whether the model explains RET with any statistical significance. She uses the partial ANOVA table results in Exhibit 1 and notes that the critical value of the F-statistic is 3.813 at the 1% significance level and 2.619 at the 5% significance level.
Exhibit 1
# Source | Degrees of Freedom | Sum of Squares | Mean Squares
Regression | 3 | 0.0453 | 0.0151
Residual | 620 | 0.9512 | 0.0015
Total | 623 | 0.9965 | ---
Next, Kendall considers platinum returns. After running the model, she tests for model misspecification. The variance inflation factor for each of the independent variables is close to 1.00, and the Breusch–Godfrey test fails to reject the null hypothesis.
Kendall considers alternate model specifications using the three factors to model platinum returns. Her objective is to select the most parsimonious, best-fitting model. Kendall evaluates several goodness-of-fit measures, including Akaike's information criterion (AIC), Schwarz's Bayesian information criteria (BIC), and R2. She gathers relevant model output in Exhibit 2.
Exhibit 2
# Model | Factors | AIC | BIC | R2
1 | FSI | 5.134 | 5.141 | 0.098
2 | FSI, GPR | 5.132 | 5.153 | 0.103
3 | FSI, GPR, EPU | 5.139 | 5.160 | 0.106
As a result of her firm investing in new data sources and technology, Kendall gains access to a wide range of new inputs that could be used to model the commodity market. She decides to utilize this dataset in a machine-learning algorithm with the goal of predicting commodity returns from the complex non-linear data.

questions.q: Do the independent variables jointly contribute to the explanation of silver returns?
options: Yes, at the 5% significance level only
Yes, at both the 5% and 1% significance levels
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because the joint contribution is tested using the F-statistic for the overall model. The F-statistic is calculated as F = mean square regression / mean square error = MSR/MSE = 0.0151/0.0015 ≈ 10. This exceeds the critical value at the 5% and 1% significance levels. 
This response would be chosen if F were calculated as mean square error / mean square regression = MSE/MSR = 0.0015/0.0151 ≈ 0.1.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because the joint contribution is tested using the F-statistic for the overall model. The F-statistic is calculated as F = mean square regression / mean square error = MSR/MSE = 0.0151/0.0015 ≈ 10. This exceeds the critical value at the 5% and 1% significance levels. 
This response would be chosen if F were calculated as sum of squares regression / mean square regression = SSR/MSR = 0.0453/0.0151 = 3.
C. Correct.

questions.q: Does the testing of the platinum return model indicate model misspecification?
options: Yes, because there is evidence of multicollinearity
Yes, because there is evidence of serial correlation
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because each variance inflation factor is close to 1. We can use the variance inflation factor (VIF) to quantify multicollinearity issues and only VIF > 5 warrants further investigation of the given independent variable.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because the results of the Breusch–Godfrey test do not reject the null hypothesis.
The null hypothesis of the Breusch–Godfrey test is that there is no serial correlation in the model's residuals up to lag p.

questions.q: Which of the models for platinum returns should Kendall select based on her objective?
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because Model 2 has the lowest Akaike's information criterion (AIC), which is preferred if the model is used for prediction purposes. However, BIC is preferred when the best goodness of fit is desired and Model 2 does not have the lowest BIC.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because Model 3 has the highest R2 but this is not generally suitable for testing the significance of the model's fit. The R2 cannot tell whether the model fit is good. BIC is preferred when the best goodness of fit is desired and Model 3 does not have the lowest BIC.
In addition, as both the R2 and adjusted R2 may increase when we add independent variables, we risk model overfitting.

questions.q: Which of the following machine-learning algorithms is best suited to Kendall's goal?
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because support vector machines are useful for classification of linear data but Kendall's goal is to predict future returns using complex non-linear data. If the problem is one of classification, then depending on whether the data are labeled, the choice is either from a set of classification algorithms using labeled data or from a set of clustering algorithms using unlabeled data. If the data are labeled, then the choice of classification algorithm would be K-nearest neighbor and support vector machine for linear data.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because principal components analysis (PCA) is best suited to dimension reduction but Kendall's goal is to predict future returns using complex non-linear data.
Dimension reduction aims to represent a dataset with many typically correlated features by a smaller set of features that still does well in describing the data. PCA is used to summarize or transform highly correlated features of data into a few main, uncorrelated composite variables.

vignettes.body:
Amanda Glade is an analyst with an investment management firm that actively manages several diversified portfolios. She is currently updating her analysis of investment markets in Country A and Country B, both of which have developed economies, and assessing portfolio performance in preparation for a report to the firm's portfolio managers.
Glade notes that Country A has a large positive equity risk premium, and she considers what this suggests about investor expectations.
Glade analyzes the breakeven inflation rate of Country B. She examines the following most recent financial data for the country:
Current yield on a 5-year zero-coupon default-free nominal bond: 4.5%
Current yield on a 5-year zero-coupon default-free real bond: 2.0%
Risk premium for inflation uncertainty: 0.3%
Next, Glade assesses the performance of the firm's actively managed global asset portfolio. Using the most recent financial information presented in Exhibit 1, she calculates the value added to the portfolio from asset allocation.
Exhibit 1
#  | Portfolio Return (%) | Benchmark Return (%) | Current Allocation (%) | Strategic Asset Allocation (%)
Global equities | 16.4 | 12.8 | 74 | 70
Global fixed income | –3.4 | –4.5 | 26 | 30
Glade considers the possibility of combining one of the firm's actively managed domestic equity funds, Fund X, with an investment in its passive index benchmark portfolio. Using the information in Exhibit 2, she determines the maximum Sharpe ratio that a portfolio manager could achieve by combining Fund X with the passive index benchmark portfolio.
Exhibit 2
#  | Index | Fund X
Sharpe ratio | 0.275 | 0.242
Active return | --- | 1.5%
Active risk | --- | 6.0%

questions.q: Country A's equity risk premium most likely suggests that investors expect equity returns and the marginal value of future consumption to be:
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because a large positive equity risk premium suggests that investors expect the marginal value of future consumption and equity returns to be negatively correlated. An equity risk premium of zero would suggest that the marginal value of future consumption and equity returns are uncorrelated.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because a large positive equity risk premium suggests that investors expect the marginal value of future consumption and equity returns to be negatively correlated. A negative (not positive) equity risk premium would suggest that the marginal value of future consumption and equity returns are positively correlated.

questions.q: Based on the most recent financial data, Country B's breakeven inflation rate is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because this answer choice incorrectly subtracts the risk premium for inflation uncertainty (0.3%) from the difference between the current yield on a 5-year zero-coupon default-free nominal bond (4.5%) and the current yield on a 5-year zero-coupon default-free real bond (2.0%).
The difference between the yield on, for example, a zero-coupon default-free nominal bond and on a zero-coupon default-free real bond of the same maturity is known as the break-even inflation (BEI) rate. It should be clear from the discussion earlier that this break-even inflation rate will incorporate the inflation expectations of investors over the investment horizon of the two bonds, plus a risk premium that will be required by investors to compensate them predominantly for uncertainty about future inflation.
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because this answer choice incorrectly adds the risk premium for inflation uncertainty (0.3%) to the difference between the current yield on a 5-year zero-coupon default-free nominal bond (4.5%) and the current yield on a 5-year zero-coupon default-free real bond (2.0%).
The difference between the yield on, for example, a zero-coupon default-free nominal bond and on a zero-coupon default-free real bond of the same maturity is known as the break-even inflation (BEI) rate. It should be clear from the discussion earlier that this break-even inflation rate will incorporate the inflation expectations of investors over the investment horizon of the two bonds, plus a risk premium that will be required by investors to compensate them predominantly for uncertainty about future inflation.

questions.q: The value added to the global asset portfolio from asset allocation is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because this is the value added from the security selection (not asset allocation) decision. The value added from security selection is calculated as the sum of the actual portfolio weights multiplied by each sub-portfolio’s value added measure. Thus, the value added from the security selection decision is: (74% × [16.4% – 12.8%]) + (26% × [–3.4% – (–4.5%)]) = 2.664% + 0.286% = 2.95%.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because this is the total value added from the asset allocation and security selection decisions: 0.692% + 2.950% = 3.642% ≈ 3.64%.
Total value added is also computed as the portfolio return minus the benchmark return: ([74% × 16.4%] + [26% × (–3.4%)]) – ([70% × 12.8%] + [30% × (–4.5%)]) = 11.252% – 7.610% = 3.642% ≈ 3.64%.

questions.q: The maximum Sharpe ratio that can be achieved by combining Fund X with an investment in its passive index benchmark portfolio is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because this is the information ratio of Fund X (active return/active risk = 1.5%/6.0%), not the maximum Sharpe ratio that can be achieved by combining Fund X with an investment in its passive index benchmark portfolio.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because this is the Sharpe ratio of the passive index benchmark portfolio (0.275 ≈ 0.28), but it is not the maximum Sharpe ratio that can be achieved by combining Fund X with an investment in its passive index benchmark portfolio.
C. Correct.

vignettes.body:
Alice Kent, a fixed-income analyst, is evaluating several bonds for potential addition to her firm's portfolios.
Kent reviews newly issued Bond X, a 3-year default-free bond with an annual coupon of 5.85% that is callable at its par value of 100 one year and two years from today. She assumes interest rate volatility of 15% and constructs the binomial interest rate tree shown in Exhibit 1. In the tree, branching from each node to a high state or a low state occurs with equal probability. Kent uses the tree to value Bond X.
Exhibit 1 Binomial Interest Rate Tree (1-year rates)
# | Year 0 | Year 1 | Year 2
Upper node |  | 4.2530% | 10.4577%
Middle node | 6.10% |  | 7.7472%
Lower node |  | 3.1507% | 5.7393%
Note: This exhibit was a binomial diagram in the original paper. Its figure was not in the pasted text: the rates are taken from the answer explanation of Question 41 (Year 0: 6.10%; Year 1: 4.2530% and 3.1507%; Year 2: 10.4577%, 7.7472% and 5.7393%); their placement in the table is a reconstruction.
Kent compares Bond X to Bond Y, a 3-year default-free putable bond with the same coupon. She expects interest rate volatility to decrease in the future and determines how the values of the two bonds would change if her expectation is realized.
Kent wants to develop a more flexible model than the binomial tree. She uses the Monte Carlo method to simulate various potential interest rate paths, with a 30-year default-free coupon-paying bond as the benchmark bond. After the initial simulation of the paths, she customizes the model by adding a constant to all interest rates on all paths to ensure that the average present value for the benchmark bond equals its current market price.
Lastly, Kent gathers information on a convertible bond that was issued at par two years ago and has three years to maturity. The bond has a par value of $1,000, a 4.90% coupon payable annually, and a conversion price of $17.77 per share. Currently the bond's price is $1,198 and the price of the underlying shares is $20.

questions.q: The value of Bond X is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because this response only reflects the exercise of the call option in Year 2. The calculations are: 
 
Values at Year 2
Top node: (100 + 5.85) / 1.104577 = $95.8285
Middle node: (100 + 5.85) / 1.077472 = $98.2392
Bottom node: (100 + 5.85) / 1.057393 = $100.1047, so the bond would be called at 100
 
Values at Year 1
Top node: [5.85 + (0.5 × 95.8285 + 0.5 × 98.2392)] / (1.042530) = $98.6867
Bottom node: [5.85 + (0.5 × 98.2392 + 0.5 × 100.0000)] / (1.031507) = $101.7633
 
Values at Year 0
Current node: [5.85 + (0.5 × 98.6867 + 0.5 × 101.7633)] / (1.0610) = $99.9764 ≈ $99.98
 
This response is also closest to the result of ignoring the call option completely, which is $100.00.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because this response reflects the exercise of a put option, rather than a call option, at the appropriate nodes in Year 1 and Year 2. The calculations are: 
 
Values at Year 2
Top node: (100 + 5.85) / 1.104577 = $95.8285, so the bond would be put at 100
Middle node: (100 + 5.85) / 1.077472 = $98.2392, so the bond would be put at 100
Bottom node: (100 + 5.85) / 1.057393 = $100.1047
 
Values at Year 1
Top node: [5.85 + (0.5 × 100.0000 + 0.5 × 100.0000)] / (1.042530) = $101.5319
Bottom node: [5.85 + (0.5 × 100.0000 + 0.5 × 100.1047)] / (1.031507) = $102.6676
 
Values at Year 0
Current node: [5.85 + (0.5 × 101.5319 + 0.5 × 102.6676)] / (1.0610) = $101.7433 ≈ $101.74

questions.q: If Kent's expectation for interest rate volatility is realized, which of the following bonds would most likely decrease in value?
options: Both Bond X and Bond Y
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Incorrect because Kent's expectation is that interest rate volatility will decrease, which will increase the value of Bond X as a result of the embedded short call option. All else being equal, the call option increases in value with interest rate volatility as interest rate volatility increases, the value of the callable bond decreases. Conversely, when interest rate volatility decreases, the value of the callable bond increases.
Value of callable bond = Value of straight bond – Value of issuer call option
B. Correct.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because Kent's expectation is that interest rate volatility will decrease, which will increase the value of callable Bond X and decrease the value of putable Bond Y.

questions.q: The technique used by Kent to customize the Monte Carlo model is best described as:
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because mean reversion is implemented by implementing upper and lower bounds on the random process generating future interest rates. Mean reversion has the effect of moving the interest rate toward the implied forward rates from the yield curve. No adjustment involving adding a constant to all rates on all paths is required.
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because the benchmark term structure is represented by the current spot curve such that the average present value across all scenario interest rate paths for each benchmark bond equals its actual market value.

questions.q: The current market conversion premium per share for the convertible bond is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Correct.
B. Incorrect. Incorrect because this response is derived from the current share price less the conversion price, which does not reflect the change in the convertible bond's price since issuance:
Incorrect market conversion premium per share = Current share price – Conversion price
where
Current share price  = $20
Conversion price = $17.77
= $20 – $17.77
= $2.23
C. Incorrect. Incorrect because this response uses the conversion price instead of the current share price:  
Incorrect market conversion premium per share = (Convertible bond price / Conversion ratio) – Conversion price
where
Convertible bond price = $1,198
Conversion ratio = (Par value / Conversion price) = $1,000 / $17.77 = 56.2746
Conversion price = $17.77
= ($1,198 / 56.2746) – $17.77
= $21.2884 – $17.77
= $3.5184 ≈ $3.52
